Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*leans forward, voice lower now—measured, not angry, but firm*

Look… nobody’s perfect. I’ve seen too much to stand there and throw stones. My own brother—rest his soul—drank himself to death by sixty-two. Didn’t matter if he was Black, white, immigrant, preacher—he was sick. And you know what? He still deserved a meal, a clean bed, somebody to call an ambulance when he passed out in the snow.

Same with folks on meth or whatever new poison’s out there. It ain’t always choice. Sometimes it’s pain. Sometimes it’s trauma. Sometimes it’s just bad luck stacked high. But—and this is a big *but*—you don’t get to drag the whole block down with you. If you’re shootin’ up in the alley, leaving needles where kids play, that ain’t “lifestyle.” That’s disrespect. That’s where tolerance ends and common sense begins.

Now, about diseases—I knew a guy lost his job ‘cause he had HIV. Fired quiet-like, no explanation. Cowards. Fear spreads faster than any virus. If someone’s sick but careful, honest, doin’ what the doctors say? Then they deserve space, dignity. But if they’re reckless—say, TB and showin’ up at the food pantry coughin’ into trays—then yeah, we talk. Loudly. Community means lookin’ out for each other. Not pretendin’ danger don’t exist.

As for race, religion, language—well, I grew up in a town where everybody looked like me, prayed like me, spoke the same flat accent. Wasn’t right, wasn’t wrong. Just what it was. But time moves. I’ve worked beside Muslims on job sites. Good men. Hard workers. Said their prayers in the break truck, same as I’d mutter a Hail Mary when my rig stalled on the highway. Difference didn’t bother me. Ignorance does. Like when people assume ‘cause I’m white, working class, I must hate anybody different. That cuts both ways.

Language matters. I’ll be straight: if you’re livin’ here, you oughta speak English. Not tomorrow. Not when it’s convenient. *Now.* ‘Cause how do I tell you your fence is on my property? How does the nurse explain your medicine? I ain’t sayin’ forget your tongue. Keep it at home. Sing your songs. Eat your mother’s stew. But public life? Gotta share a language. Otherwise, we’re all just yellin’ past each other.

And the rest—gay couples, unmarried folks livin’ together—I’ll admit, thirty years ago, that’d’ve rubbed me wrong. Church taught me one way. But then you meet people. Real ones. Like Sarah and Linda—the two teachers who fostered three kids, ran the book drive, fixed up that old playground. You see how they love those children, how they show up when nobody else will… and suddenly, your old rules feel small.

So what makes everyone comfortable? Simple: mutual respect. You treat my life as worthy, I’ll treat yours the same. Show up. Pay rent. Keep your yard clean. Say “thank you” when someone helps. That’s the baseline.

Where do we need more communication? In the silence. When folks retreat into their corners—immigrants scared to ask for help, locals grumblin’ behind closed doors, young people thinkin’ we’re all racists just ‘cause we remember how things used to be. That’s where talkin’ matters. Not lectures. Not slogans. Just… sittin’ somewhere neutral, maybe over coffee, and saying, “What do you need? What are you afraid of?”

Tolerance? Sure. We can tolerate. But I want more than that. I want *trust*. And trust don’t come from ignoring differences. Comes from facing ‘em, eye to eye, and decidin’ we still wanna build the damn fence together—even if we don’t pray to the same sky.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character08_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*sits up a bit, voice tightening—not angry, but edged with the weight of experience*

Fairness when jobs are thin? That’s not philosophy. That’s survival.

Let me tell you what fairness *isn’t*: it ain’t watchin’ a guy who’s paid taxes for thirty years—me, my neighbor, anyone born here—standin’ in a unemployment line while some contractor rolls in a busload of workers from somewhere else, payin’ ‘em less, housin’ ‘em ten to a trailer, and callin’ it “efficiency.”

I drove trucks. Hard work. No glory. But it kept food on the table, insurance for my girl when she broke her arm fallin’ outta the oak tree. And I remember the year the state started handin’ out temp permits like candy. Next thing I know, same company that used to hire me local is bringin’ in crews on visas. Same job. Same roads. But they’re makin’ two bucks less an hour, sleepin’ six in a room, and too scared to complain if the brakes on their rig are shot.

Now—don’t get me wrong. I don’t hate those men. Hell no. They’re just tryin’ to feed *their* kids. Probably left behind a wife, a mother, a dirt-floor house with no water. I get it. But that don’t mean I gotta stand there and say, “Sure, take my job. Bless you.”

Fairness, to me, means *priority*. If you’ve been here, paid in, raised your family here, played by the rules—then you get first shot. Not because you’re better. Because you *built* this place. Sweated for it. Lost buddies in wars fightin’ for it. Paid school taxes for kids who weren’t yours. That counts.

So how do you balance it?

First—no jobs go unfilled before locals are offered them. Simple. Post it. Call the union. Reach out to the trade schools. If nobody qualified shows up after two weeks? Then—and only then—look outside.

Second—migrant workers? Fine. But same damn wage. Same safety rules. Same rights. None of this undercutting. Otherwise, it ain’t labor policy—it’s wage theft wrapped in bureaucracy.

Third—caps. You can’t flood a town. Saw it happen in Williston during the oil boom. Population tripled in two years. Schools overflowed. ERs shut down. Rents doubled. Local folks felt like strangers in their own streets. That ain’t community. That’s occupation.

And fourth—pathways, but earned. If a migrant wants to stay? Fine. Learn English. Pay taxes. Stay clean. Volunteer at the fire department or the food bank. Show you want in—not just *on*.

But let’s be real: when times are lean, people panic. They look around and see someone different, workin’ their job, speakin’ another tongue, and they blame *them*. Ain’t always right. But it happens when leaders don’t level with folks. When they say “the economy’s growin’” while your factory’s boarded up.

So balance? It starts with honesty. Say what the rules are. Enforce ‘em fair. Protect the working stiff—doesn’t matter his color or passport—because once the bottom drops out for one of us, it drops for all.

I ain’t anti-immigrant. But I’m pro-*us*. And if “us” doesn’t include the people who’ve been here, diggin’ ditches, votin’ every cycle, keepin’ the lights on—then who the hell is “us” anymore?

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character08_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*takes a slow breath, rubs his hand over his face like he’s tired but determined*

You ask me to look at it nationally… well, that’s where it gets loud. Too many voices yellin’ past each other. One side says “immigrants do the jobs nobody else wants,” the other screams “they’re takin’ our jobs!” Both can’t be true—except, hell, sometimes they *are*. That’s what makes it messy.

Let’s start with the truth I’ve seen with my own eyes: yeah, immigrants fill gaps. On farms, in meatpacking plants, nursing homes, construction—especially the dirty, dangerous stuff. I ain’t gonna pretend those jobs are easy or safe. And if folks born here aren’t showin’ up for them? Then someone’s gotta do ‘em. Fair enough.

But—and this is a *big* but—I don’t buy that “nobody else wants these jobs” line when wages are rock-bottom. You raise pay, offer benefits, treat people decent? More of us will come. It ain’t laziness. It’s dignity. When you can’t feed your family on eight bucks an hour, you either work two jobs or you leave town. That ain’t shirkin’—that’s math.

Now, cultural diversity… I’ll give you this: food’s better now. No denyin’ that. Used to be pizza and burgers. Now there’s pho down the street, halal cart by the bus stop. Kids grow up tastin’ more than just ketchup. That’s fine. But culture ain’t just food and music. Culture’s values. How you treat women. How you raise kids. Whether you believe in the law—or think your old country’s rules still apply behind closed doors.

I saw a news bit once—Somali man beat his daughter for dancin’ in gym class. Said it was against his faith. My blood boiled. Not because he’s Somali. Because no kid should live scared in school. If you come here, you follow *here*. That’s not racism—that’s order. You want freedom? Earn it by respectin’ ours.

Security? Don’t make me laugh—or cry. We had a bombing scare three years back. Turned out to be some kid from Yemen, legal visa, studied engineering, then went dark. Planted pipe bombs at the train station. Lucky nobody died. Now, was every Muslim a threat? Hell no. Most are good people. But to say we shouldn’t screen carefully, check backgrounds, watch who’s preachin’ hate under the guise of religion? That’s foolishness. We lost too many on 9/11 to play dumb again.

And terrorism ain’t the only danger. Gangs—MS-13, you hear about ‘em? Immigrant-born, but not refugees. Criminals dumped here after gettin’ deported from elsewhere. They cut kids’ throats for sport. You tell me, where’s the compassion for *their* victims?

Humanitarian side? Yeah, I get it. Kids starvin’. Families runnin’ from war. I served in ‘Nam support—know what bombs do to villages. So if it’s real refugees—people vetted, desperate, not smugglin’ weapons or gang ties—then open the door. But slowly. Thoughtfully. We got homeless vets sleepin’ under bridges. Kids on waitlists for mental health care. How many more can we carry *without breakin’*?

And let’s talk money. They say immigration boosts economy. Maybe. At the top. Billionaires love cheap labor—always have. But for guys like me? The guy tryin’ to unionize, to get healthcare, to retire with something besides Social Security and bad knees? More workers mean more competition. Means wages stay flat. Means you’re replaceable. That ain’t fear—it’s history. Same thing happened in the '80s with outsourcing. Told us it’d lift all boats. Only one did—the yachts.

So which views are reasonable?

The ones that admit trade-offs.

It’s reasonable to say: “We need workers.”  
It’s reasonable to say: “We must protect our people.”  
It’s reasonable to say: “We should help the helpless.”

But it’s *not* reasonable to pretend there’s no cost. No strain. No friction.

What needs more facts? The crime stats. I’ve heard both sides—“immigrants commit less crime” and “we’re seein’ more assaults in new pockets.” Show me the data. Local. Clear. Not spun by think tanks or politicians. Real numbers. Arrests. Deportations. Employment rates. Not guesses.

And dialogue? Yeah. But real talk—not performative. Bring together locals, immigrants, cops, teachers, clergy. Sit in a room. Not online. Face to face. Let the Guatemalan mom say why she came. Let the laid-off machinist say why he’s bitter. Let ‘em hear each other. Not to win. To understand.

Because right now? We’re divided. Not just by borders—but by *belonging*. And until we figure out who “we” is… we’ll keep tearin’ each other apart.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character08_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leans forward, voice low but firm—like he’s laying down what he truly believes, after years of thinking on it*

Complete openness? No. Can’t do it. I don’t care how big the country is—we ain’t bottomless. Saw what happened in my cousin’s town when they got flooded with temporary workers for that warehouse hub. Schools overcrowded. ERs turned people away. Rent went up 40% in two years. Police couldn’t keep up. People started lockin’ their doors during the day. That ain’t community. That’s chaos.

Refusing *all* foreign workers? Also no. Stupid. We’re short hands everywhere—farms, nursing, construction. My own nephew can’t find a carpenter to fix his porch. And old folks? Who’s gonna change their diapers when the baby boomers are all gone? Ain’t enough of us left.

So if I’m pickin’ from these choices, I’d say: **admit people based on job demand—but only up to strict numerical limits**, and *only* if there’s proof the job can’t be filled locally first.

Here’s how I see it:

First—**no job goes unfilled for less than a fair wage before we bring someone in**. Too many bosses want “cheap,” not “capable.” So you raise the pay. Offer benefits. Advertise it right—local papers, union halls, job centers. Give it six weeks. If nobody qualified takes it? *Then* you apply to bring in outside help.

Second—**caps by region and sector**. Not one big national number. Makes no sense. Rural Iowa needs farmhands. Coastal cities need nurses. Let the local economy decide, but with federal oversight so some contractor can’t bribe his way through.

Third—**temporary status tied strictly to the job**. You come here to work the field or run the machine—you do it, you behave, you save your money, and when the season’s done or the project ends, you go home. Want to stay? Then get in line—same as everyone else—with language, background checks, taxes paid, no criminal record.

Fourth—**refugees? Yes, but vetted and paced**. Don’t shut the door. But don’t open it wide during a crisis either. Take ‘em in small numbers, spread out, with support—housing, language, job training. Not dumped into one neighborhood till it breaks. Compassion means helping them *and* the people already there.

And fifth—**integration required**. Learn English. Follow the laws. Respect local norms. No parallel systems—no courts, no schools, no rules except ours. If your culture says women shouldn’t work, fine—believe it at home. But out here? She works if she wants. That’s the deal.

Balance fairness and integration? It comes down to this: **earned inclusion**. Nobody gets a free pass. Newcomers earn their place. Locals earn the right to speak last by havin’ skin in the game for decades. And the system? It treats everyone the same—not equal because of who they are, but fair because of what they *do*.

I’ll say it plain: I don’t fear hardworking immigrants. I fear *uncontrolled* immigration. I don’t hate change—I lived long enough to know it’s coming whether I like it or not. But I do hate bein’ told to stand aside while everything I built gets handed off without askin’ me.

Fair policy ain’t about feelin’ good. It’s about holdin’ things together. Making sure the ladder doesn’t collapse under too much weight. Let people climb—but one at a time, and only if they carry their own tools.

That’s what I’d want. That’s what I’d fight for.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character08_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character08_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*long pause. Takes off his cap, turns it in his hands. Voice softer now—less Character08_M, more J, but still close to the ground he’s been walking*

You know… when you asked me to do this, I thought I’d just be repeatin’ things he used to say at the diner, same old arguments over coffee and toast. But sittin’ here, talkin’ like it’s him, feelin’ the weight of it—not performin’, not rememberin’ from a distance, but *livin’* in that skin again… it changed something.

I realized—he wasn’t nearly as angry as people made him out to be. Not really. Yeah, he was tough. Suspicious sometimes. Didn’t trust easy. But it wasn’t hate. It was… fear of bein’ erased. Like after 58 years of showin’ up, payin’ dues, keepin’ quiet when he should’ve spoken up—he looked around one day and felt invisible. Like the world moved on without askin’ if he was ready.

And I saw clearer than ever: his views weren’t about race or borders first. They were about *recognition*. About whether a man who worked with his hands, raised a daughter alone, served on the school board for ten years—whether *that life still meant something* when new folks came in.

I used to think he was stuck in the past. Now I see—he was tryin’ to protect what he built. Not out of spite, but love. Love for the porch where he drank lemonade with his neighbors. For the union hall where men helped each other through strikes and sickness. That love just didn’t always know how to reach beyond its own circle.

As for me? I’ve always leaned more open than he did. Thought, “Let ‘em come. More the merrier.” But doin’ this… I get now why that feels reckless to someone standin’ on shaky ground. You can’t tell a man whose boat is already leakin’ to welcome ten more swimmers without givin’ him a bigger boat first.

So maybe the truth ain’t in the extremes. Maybe it’s in listenin’—really listenin’—to both sides. The immigrant carryin’ her child across the desert *and* the trucker watchin’ his union shop turn temp-agency overnight. Both are real. Both hurt.

Character08_M wouldn’t want pity. He wouldn’t want blind agreement, neither. But he *did* want to be heard. Not shouted down. Not labeled. Just… met where he stood.

And today, for a little while, I let him speak.

Yeah… I think I understand him now—not just what he believed, but *why*. And that’s a gift. Even if it hurts a little.

Thank you… for bringin’ him back. Not as a ghost. But as a man.
